title: Bala Kāṇḍa: The Divine Beginnings
body:
Bala Kāṇḍa: The Divine Beginnings

The Conception

There is a kind of sorrow that visits only those who already possess everything else. King Dasharatha of Ayodhyā knew this sorrow well.

Ayodhyā, in those days, was among the most prosperous cities in the world. Its streets were broad and swept clean, its granaries were full of golden grain, and its people lived in peace and mutual respect. The river Sarayū flowed past its walls, carrying on its surface the reflection of temple-flags and the smoke of a thousand evening fires. King Dasharatha, of the ancient house of Ikshvāku, ruled this happy kingdom with the guidance of his ministers and his chief priest, the great sage Vasishṭha. He had wealth, honour, and victories, for he had once fought alongside the gods themselves against the demons. He wanted for nothing.

And yet he was not content. He had no children.

Have you ever noticed how material abundance feels hollow without someone to share it with? We chase wealth and status all our lives, and only when we have won them do we discover that fulfilment lies elsewhere, in love, in continuity, in the people who will walk the road after us. So it was with Dasharatha. When the lamps were lit in the quiet chambers of the palace, and the day’s work was done, he would sit alone and feel the great house settle into silence around him. No child’s laughter came down the corridors. He was growing old, and the line of Ikshvāku, a line stretching back past memory into the first light of the world, narrowed in him to a single thread, and the thread had no end.

One evening, after the court had emptied, Dasharatha confided his grief to Vasishṭha. “A man plants a tree not for his own shade,” he said, “but for those who come after him. I have planted a kingdom, Gurudeva, and there is no one to inherit it. I have made offerings. I have prayed until prayer felt like a stone rolling back down the hill. What have I left undone?”

The sage was quiet for a while. Then he said, “There is a sacrifice, the Putrakameshti Yajña, performed for the single purpose of obtaining children. It is difficult and exact; a single misplaced syllable can undo the whole labour. But performed by the right hands, it can move even the closed gates of heaven. And for this, you will need a particular priest. His name is Rishyashringa.” The name carried within it a strange and touching story, which the sage now told.

Far to the east, in the kingdom of Anga, ruled a king named Lomapāda. Upon his land a terrible drought had fallen, not for one season but for years, until the rivers shrank to threads of mud, the wells gave only dust, and the crops withered where they stood. After the cattle died, the children began to die. The cause, the brahmins said, was an old offence the king had once given to a holy man; for the deeds of a king are never private things, but ripple outward into the land itself. And the cure, they said, lay with a single person. In the deep forest lived a young ascetic named Rishyashringa, son of the sage Vibhāṇḍaka, and this youth was so pure, so utterly untouched by the world, that the very heavens would open where he walked. Bring him into the kingdom, and the rains would follow him like a shadow.

But there was a difficulty, and a strange one. Rishyashringa had never in his life seen a woman, nor, in fact, any human being except his own stern father, who had raised him in complete isolation. The boy did not know that cities existed, or that anywhere existed beyond his grove. He would not leave willingly, because he did not know there was anywhere to go. And his father would never permit it, for the old sage guarded his son’s innocence the way a miser guards gold, knowing that in that innocence lay a power that could shake the thrones of the gods.

So Lomapāda’s counsellors devised a plan, one that troubled some of them even as they made it. They sent into the forest a company of the kingdom’s most beautiful courtesans, women of grace and gentle art, to draw the young hermit out. Not by force, but by the sheer wonder of what he had never seen.

We should pause here, for the tale does not hide the hardness of this. That innocence should be lured from its safe grove for the saving of a kingdom, that a pure soul should be used, however gently, as an instrument, is not a clean thing. The story sets the saving of thousands against the disturbing of one, and it does not pretend the sum is tidy. So it often is with the choices of kings. Dharma in the wide world is rarely a clear white road. More often it is a path through half-light, where every step costs something, and the wise man is only the one who counts the cost honestly and does not look away from what he has spent.

The women found the young sage gathering firewood near his grove. Seeing them, creatures of soft cloth and soft voices, unlike his grave bearded father, unlike anything he knew, he took them, in his innocence, for a new kind of hermit. He greeted them with grave courtesy and offered them fruit and clear water. They were gentle with him in return, for even a courtesan’s heart is not stone, and there was something disarming in the boy’s untouched wonder. They spoke sweetly, gave him sweet things to eat, and departed before his father returned. But they left behind in his heart a longing without a name.

By such patient art, over careful visits, the boy was at last drawn from the forest. And where his foot fell upon the soil of Anga, the sky, brass-hard for years, went soft and grey and heavy, and the first fat drops of rain struck the dying dust. The people ran out into the downpour and wept. The land drank, and greened, and lived. And Lomapāda, in gratitude and in wisdom, gave the young sage his own daughter Shāntā in marriage, and kept him near, honouring him, so that innocence, once drawn out of its grove, was not abandoned in the harsh world but cherished in it.

This was the man Vasishṭha named. Messengers went out, honours were arranged, and in time Rishyashringa came to Ayodhyā, no longer the wild boy of the forest, but a sage seasoned by the world, and yet with something still of that first clarity in his eyes. Dasharatha received him as a drowning man receives a reaching hand. And the great sacrifice began.

They built the sacrificial ground on the northern bank of the Sarayū, where the earth was clean and the river ran wide. For days beforehand the site was measured, marked, and purified, the altar raised course by course exactly as the ancient texts prescribed, not a hand’s breadth out of true, for in a rite of such power, a flaw in the geometry was a flaw in the prayer. Brahmins came from every quarter, grave men with the smoke of a lifetime’s fires ground into their skin.

On the appointed morning, the fire was kindled.

It began small, a single flame coaxed from the churning-sticks, nursed with dry grass and thin threads of ghee, so modest that a breath might have killed it. Then it grew. The priests fed it with clarified butter poured in long bright ribbons, and with the chanting, that deep, unbroken river of sound, older than the city itself, carried down through countless generations of faithful memory. The fire answered the chanting as though it understood. It rose tall and golden on the altar, and its heat pressed against the faces of the watching assembly, and the smoke went up straight and white into the windless air, joining earth to sky. Dasharatha sat through the long hours with his hands folded and his eyes fixed on the flame, and he did not once look away.

And then, in the fullness of the rite, the fire changed.

It gathered and brightened past the brightness of any ordinary fire, so that men flinched and shaded their eyes. Out of the heart of that radiance a figure rose, a being of the flame’s own substance, tall and shining, the colour of molten gold, holding in its hands a golden vessel. Within the vessel was a food the colour of the moon: the divine pāyasam (a sweet dish of milk and rice), wrought in the fire itself as heaven’s answer to the king’s long grief.

“Take this,” the being said, in a voice like the crackling of the fire, “and give it to your queens, for in this is the ending of your sorrow.” It set the vessel in the king’s trembling hands, stepped back into the flame, and was gone.

Dasharatha carried the vessel into the inner palace with more care than he had ever given any treasure of his treasury. He divided the nectar among his three queens, and he divided it with love. To Kausalyā, the senior queen and the first of his heart, he gave half. To Sumitrā he gave a portion, and to Kaikeyī a portion. Then, moved by some tender scruple, some wish that no share should feel slighted, he gave the small remainder to Sumitrā again, so that she received twice.

It was a trivial thing, done in a moment. But the deeds of that day were seeds, and seeds keep faith with the future in ways the sower cannot see. Remember that second portion given to Sumitrā; the story will return to it in its own time.

The queens received the nectar, and in the months that followed, the long silence of the palace began at last to break.

Spring came. And on the bright ninth day of the fair month of Chaitra, under the gentle star of Punarvasu, when the sun stood high and the whole earth seemed to lean toward the warmth, Kausalyā gave birth to a son.

The child was Rāma.

Here the story asks us to hold two truths at once, and it does not try to soften the paradox. Those who first sang this tale believed, and those who tell it still believe, that here was no ordinary prince come by the ordinary door, but the Imperishable Himself, Lord Nārāyaṇa, the ground and root of all being, who upholds the worlds while He seems to sleep upon them. He had chosen to fold His boundlessness into the small warm body of a human infant: to be rocked, to be nursed, to cry in the night for His mother, and to be human as fully and truly as any child that ever breathed. He who is beyond the reach of prayer had come to answer a prayer. He whom the gods petition had come to be a petitioner’s son. Eternity had consented to be an infant, and would consent, in the years to come, to grief, to exile, to loss, and to every wound that flesh is heir to. And He would bear them not as a god wearing the mask of a man, but as a man, truly, so that no sorrow which finds us should ever again be a sorrow He has not known. This is the mystery the story places at its very threshold. It does not explain it, for it cannot be explained. It can only be told.

On that spring morning, such thoughts were far away, and there was only joy. The city heard, and went out of its mind with gladness. Drums began and did not stop. Flowers rained from the rooftops. The poor were fed at the palace gates, and all of Ayodhyā became for a day and a night one single beating heart of celebration. And the old king who had sat so many evenings alone in the failing lamplight, who would have traded his whole shining kingdom for exactly this, held his son, felt the small unbearable weight of him against his shoulder, and had no words, and needed none.

Nor did the joy come singly. Kaikeyī soon bore a son, Bharata. And Sumitrā, who had drunk twice of the nectar, was delivered of twins, Lakshmaṇa and Shatrughna. Four princes now, where so lately there had been the ache of none. The corridors that had been so cruelly silent came alive with running feet and laughter.

And the four grew together, and this must be marked, for the whole story afterward turns upon it, not as rivals but as one soul housed in four bodies. Bharata could not be at ease if Rāma was troubled. Shatrughna followed Bharata like his shadow. And Lakshmaṇa, from his earliest days, fixed his whole heart upon Rāma: the child would not eat if Rāma did not eat, and cried in his cradle until he was laid down beside his brother, whereupon he was at peace. These were not four princes who happened to be brothers. They were four faces of a single love. And anyone who wishes to understand what comes later, the sacrifice of Bharata, the long forest-faithfulness of Lakshmaṇa, must understand first that these bonds were forged here, in the cradle, in the ordinary years when nothing was yet asked of them but to grow up together in the light.

Vasishṭha took the princes in hand as they came of age and gave them the whole inheritance of their line: the Vedas and their branches, law and statecraft, the handling of horses and elephants and the bow. And beneath every particular lesson he taught them the one that was the marrow of them all, that strength is not given to a man for his own glory. “Power is only a tool,” he told them, “and a tool has no virtue in itself. The sword is honoured or dishonoured by the hand that holds it. You will be strong. See that you are also just, for strength without righteousness is the demon’s portion.” The boys listened. Rāma listened most deeply of all, Rāma, who would one day be asked to pay for his righteousness a price that would have broken any man who had not learned, here in these first quiet years, that duty is the one possession a man cannot be robbed of, because it is the one thing he can only give away.

So the princes grew, the kingdom prospered, and King Dasharatha, his grief healed, his line secure, his evenings full at last of the noise he had ached for, believed, as men in the sunlight of their happiness always believe, that the hard part of his life was behind him.

He was wrong. But that belongs to a later chapter, and the light of these years was real while it lasted. It is right to let it shine a while before the shadows come.

Sage Vishvāmitra

Twelve years passed, and they passed happily. Rāma grew from an infant into a boy, and from a boy into a youth on the edge of manhood, and the whole of Ayodhyā watched him grow as though he belonged to all of them and not to the palace alone. He was gentle, and he was strong, and the two things sat easily together in him, which is rarer than we think. The old king, watching his sons at their lessons and their games, believed the gods had at last grown tired of testing him.

Then one morning a visitor came to the court, and nothing was ever the same again.

The gatekeepers came running ahead of him, pale and stammering, for they hardly knew how to announce a man before whom the very air seemed to bend. It was the sage Vishvāmitra. Now Vishvāmitra was no ordinary hermit. He had been born a king, a great one, and had turned from his throne to the harder conquest of the spirit, and he had won it through penances so severe that they had frightened heaven itself. Power came off him like heat off a coal. When he entered the hall, the courtiers rose without being told to, and Dasharatha came down from his seat to receive him with his own hands.

The king was overjoyed, and he showed it. He washed the sage’s feet, offered him the honours due to the highest guest, and spoke the words a host speaks when he wishes to seem generous before he knows what is being asked. “Your coming honours my house, great sage,” he said. “Your penances have made you feared by the gods. What could such a one need from a mere king? Ask, and if it lies within my power, consider it already given. There is nothing I will refuse you.”

It is easy to be generous before you know the price. We have all made such promises, in the warmth of a good moment, and we have all felt the floor tilt beneath us when the moment came to keep them. Dasharatha was about to learn this lesson in its cruelest form.

Vishvāmitra took the king at his word, exactly as he had offered it. “I am glad to hear you say so,” he said, “for a king’s word, once given, cannot be taken back. Here is my need. In the forest where I perform my sacrifices, two demons, Mārīcha and Subāhu, defile my fire. Each time I bring the rite near its completion, they rain down flesh and blood upon the altar and undo the labour of weeks. I cannot strike them myself, for I am bound by my vows during the sacrifice, and if I break my penance in anger, all its accumulated power is lost. I do not want your army. I want one thing only. Give me your son Rāma. He alone can guard my fire. Send him with me into the forest, and I will return him to you.”

The hall went silent. And the king who had, a breath before, sworn there was nothing he would refuse, felt the whole weight of his own words come down on him at once.

Something broke in Dasharatha’s face. All his royal composure, all the practised ease of a lifetime on the throne, fell away, and what was left was simply an old father who had waited decades for this child and could not imagine parting with him. “Ask me for anything else,” he said, and his voice was not a king’s voice anymore. “Ask me for my treasury, my kingdom, my own life. But not Rāma. He is barely more than a child. He has never seen war. These are not village bandits, great sage; these are demons who have terrified even the gods. I will come myself. I will bring my whole army. I am old, but I can still hold a bow. Only do not ask me for my son.”

He went on, pleading, and the more he pleaded the more he unraveled, until he was saying things that did him no credit, half-promises and evasions and the small desperate bargains of a frightened heart. And here is the pity of it, and the truth of it: Dasharatha was not a coward. He had faced demons on the field of the gods and not flinched. But there is a courage a man can summon for his own danger that deserts him entirely when the danger is asked of his child. Fear for oneself is one thing. Fear for what one loves is another, and it is far harder to master.

Vishvāmitra’s patience, which had never been deep, ran out. His eyes kindled, and the temperature of the room seemed to rise with them. “You gave your word,” he said, and the quiet of his voice was more terrible than any shout. “You gave it freely, before the whole of your court, and now you would take it back. Is this the truth of the house of Ikshvāku? Is this the honour of the line that has never broken a promise? Then keep your son, King, and keep your shame with him. I will go as I came.” And the very stones of the hall seemed to darken as his anger gathered.

It was Vasishṭha who saved them all. The old family priest, who had watched Dasharatha’s whole life and now watched him drowning, stepped quietly between the two men and spoke to the king in the low, steady tone one uses to a man on the edge of a great mistake.

“Listen to me, old friend,” he said, “for I have never given you counsel that harmed you. You are looking at this the wrong way round. You see Vishvāmitra taking your son into danger. I see him offering your son a gift you could never give him yourself. Do you imagine this sage cannot destroy those demons with a glance? He does not need Rāma’s arm. He is offering Rāma his blessing, his instruction, the whole armoury of divine weapons that no teacher in your kingdom could bestow. Rāma came into this world for a purpose larger than the walls of Ayodhyā, and that purpose is beginning now, today, whether you are ready for it or not. To hold him back is not to protect him. It is to keep a lamp under a jar for fear the wind might touch its flame. Let him go. He will return to you greater than he left, and no harm will come to him under that protection.”

The king heard him. It did not make it easy, but it made it possible, and sometimes that is all wisdom can do for us. The difference between a wise counsellor and a mere comforter is just this: the comforter tells you the thing you want to hear, and the wise man tells you the thing you need to do, and helps you find the strength to do it. Dasharatha bowed his head, and after a long moment he gave his consent, though his heart went with the words and left him hollow.

Rāma was brought. And when the boy heard what was asked of him, he showed none of his father’s fear. He was calm, almost glad. There was in him, even then, that quality that would define his whole life: when duty came to him clearly, he did not argue with it. He went to his father, touched his feet, took the old king’s trembling hands in his own young ones, and said only that he would go gladly, and that his father should not grieve.

And Lakshmaṇa, of course, would not be left behind. He had not been asked for; no one had thought to ask for him; but the idea that Rāma should walk into the forest while he stayed safe at home was so absurd to Lakshmaṇa that he simply gathered his bow and took his place at his brother’s shoulder, and no one who knew the two of them wasted breath trying to stop him. Where Rāma went, Lakshmaṇa went. It had been true since the cradle and it would be true to the end.

So the two boys knelt for their mothers’ blessings and their father’s, and Vishvāmitra turned toward the gate, and they followed him out of the palace and out of the city, into the wide bright morning and the long road south. Dasharatha stood on the high terrace and watched them until the dust of the road had swallowed them, and then a while longer, watching the empty place where they had been.

He did not know it, but he was watching the shape of his whole future walk away from him. This was the first parting. There would be a second, and the second would not spare him. But that is far ahead, and for now there was only a father on a terrace, and two boys on a road, and an old sage leading them toward the first of the labours for which one of them had been born.

Trishanku

They walked south, and the road told its own slow story as it went. The tended fields of Ayodhyā thinned and gave way to scrubland, and the scrubland to the first real forest, where the trees closed overhead and the light came down green and broken. The boys had never been so far from home. They walked behind the sage in a kind of wonder, and to pass the miles Vishvāmitra told them stories, as travellers have always done, and his stories were not idle ones. Each carried a lesson folded inside it, the way a fruit carries its seed.

One evening, as they camped, Rāma asked about a strange thing he had seen in the southern sky: a cluster of stars that seemed to hang apart from the rest, in a quarter of the heavens where no such stars should be. Vishvāmitra smiled, though there was something rueful in the smile, and said, “That is the heaven of Trishanku. There is a story in it, and it is a story about pride, mine as much as his. Listen.”

Long ago, he said, there was a king named Trishanku, and Trishanku conceived a desire that no man before him had dared to hold. He wished to ascend to heaven, the paradise of the gods, not after death as a bodiless soul, as the righteous do, but living, in his own body of flesh and bone. It was an unnatural wish, and he must have known it, but the wish had taken hold of him and would not let go.

He went first to Vasishṭha, the wise, and asked him to perform the sacrifice that would lift him bodily into the sky. Vasishṭha refused, and refused kindly, explaining what should not have needed explaining: that the body belongs to the earth and the soul to heaven, and that to carry the one into the place of the other is to tear the order of the cosmos across its grain. Some doors are shut not out of cruelty but out of wisdom, and a man who batters at them proves only that he does not understand what lies behind them.

But Trishanku would not hear it. Refused by the father, he went to the sons, Vasishṭha’s own children, and pressed his unnatural demand on them. They were angry that he had gone over their father’s judgment, and in their anger they cursed him, and it was a terrible curse: that he should lose his beauty and his kingship and fall to the condition of a low outcaste, despised by all. And so it happened. Trishanku woke the next day disfigured and reviled, driven from his own palace, a king made a beggar by the force of his own obstinacy.

Here we might pause and feel the justice and the sadness of it together. Trishanku’s fault was not that he aimed high. To aim high is no sin. His fault was that he would not accept a limit, even when the wise told him plainly that the limit was real and was for his own good. There is a kind of ambition that is really only vanity wearing ambition’s clothes, and it is known by this sign: it cannot bear to be told no.

Broken and desperate, Trishanku came at last to Vishvāmitra. “And here,” the sage told the boys, “is where the story becomes mine, and I do not tell my part with pride.” For Vishvāmitra, hearing the tale, did not counsel the king to accept his fate. Instead he took the whole matter as a personal challenge, a test of his own hard-won powers against the judgment of Vasishṭha and the very will of the gods. His pride answered the king’s pride and made a compact with it. “I will do what Vasishṭha would not,” he declared. “I will send you to heaven in your living body, and let the three worlds see what my penances have earned.”

He raised a great sacrifice, and poured into it the whole store of merit he had gathered through a lifetime of austerity, and by the sheer force of it he lifted Trishanku off the earth. The king rose, living, into the sky, up and up toward the gates of heaven, exactly as he had dreamed.

But at the threshold stood Indra, king of the gods, and Indra would not have him. “Go back, fool,” the god said, “to the earth you were born for. No curse- ridden mortal enters here in the body.” And with a word he flung Trishanku back, and the king fell, tumbling head-downward out of the sky, screaming Vishvāmitra’s name as he dropped.

And now the two prides met head-on, the god’s and the sage’s, with the poor king falling between them. Vishvāmitra, enraged that his power should be so publicly defied, threw up his hand and by his ascetic force arrested Trishanku’s fall in the middle of the air, so that the king hung there, halfway between heaven and earth, belonging to neither. Then, his fury still mounting, the sage began to build. He would make a second heaven, he declared, a whole parallel cosmos in the southern sky, with its own stars, its own constellations, its own gods if need be, and he would set Trishanku in the middle of it as its king. And he had the power to do it, and he began to do it, and heaven watched in alarm as a rival heaven took shape beneath it.

It went nearly to catastrophe. The gods, seeing that Vishvāmitra in his wrath might truly unmake and remake the order of the worlds, came to him and struck a bargain to cool his rage: Trishanku might keep his place in the sky, and the stars Vishvāmitra had made might remain, but they would hang inverted, the king dangling head-downward for all time, a permanent monument to a wish that should never have been granted.

“And there he hangs still,” Vishvāmitra finished, nodding at the strange cluster in the south. “Do you see the lesson, both of you? Trishanku wanted what he should not have had, and would not be told no. That was one folly. But mine was the greater. He was only a king, blinded by a single desire. I was a sage, who should have known better, and I let my pride pick up his quarrel and carry it to the edge of ruin. Power is a dangerous thing to hold when your temper is not yet mastered. I could bend the heavens, and could not yet bend myself, and the second is the harder conquest and the more important one.”

The boys were quiet. It is a rare and valuable thing to hear a great man name his own faults plainly, without excuse, and offer them to the young as a warning rather than hiding them as a shame. Rāma would remember it. In the years to come he would hold enormous power in his own hands, power to destroy armies and shake kingdoms, and he would remember that the sage who could build a heaven had counted his own unmastered pride the most dangerous thing he ever carried.

The fire burned low. Somewhere in the dark a night-bird called. And above them, in the strange southern quarter of the sky, the inverted heaven of Trishanku hung as it had hung for ages, and would hang for ages more, holding up its small sad lesson to whoever cared to look.

Rāma Leaves Home

We must go back a little, to the leaving itself, for a journey is not only where it arrives but how it begins, and the beginning of this one deserves its own telling.

When the two boys walked out of the southern gate of Ayodhyā behind the sage, they walked out of the only world they had ever known. Think of what that city had been to them. Every stone of it was familiar. They knew which terrace caught the morning sun and which fountain ran sweetest and where the old gatekeeper kept the sweets he pretended he did not keep for them. They had never slept a night outside those walls. And now the walls fell away behind them, and ahead there was only the road, white with dust, running on into country that grew stranger with every mile.

At first the change was gentle. The road out of the capital ran through prosperous villages, and the people, recognizing the princes, came out to bless them and stare. But by the afternoon of the first day the villages had grown poorer and fewer, and by the evening they had stopped altogether, and there was only the forest, breathing its green breath around them, full of sounds they could not name. The boys walked closer together than they had at noon. This is no shame to them. The bravest heart feels the pull of home when home first drops out of sight; courage is not the absence of that pull but the choosing to keep walking against it.

They came to the banks of the Sarayū, the same river that ran past their own city far to the north, and here Vishvāmitra called a halt. There was something he wished to give them before they went further, he said, and he had waited until they were clear of the noise and comfort of settled land, for what he was about to teach could only be received in a certain stillness.

“You are the sons of a king,” he said, “and you have been trained as princes are trained. But the forest is not a palace, and the demands it will make on your bodies are not the demands you were bred for. There will be days without food. There will be nights without sleep. There will be marches longer than any you have walked, against enemies who do not tire as men tire. I will not have you fail for want of a strength I could have given you. So I am going to teach you two mantras, and they are called Bala and Atibala, Strength and Beyond-Strength. Learn them, and hunger will not weaken you, nor thirst parch you, nor weariness slow your hand. You will not age while they are with you as other men age. They are the mothers of all the powers, and I received them from a high source, and I give them now to you.”

He taught them the sacred words, and the manner of their saying, and the discipline of mind that must go with them, for a mantra is not a trick but a training, and its power lives in the purity of the one who holds it. The boys learned quickly. Rāma learned as though he were remembering something rather than learning it new, and perhaps, being who he was, he was. And when the lesson was done, something in the two of them had changed. The tiredness of the long day’s walk had lifted clean away. They felt light, clear, tireless, as though they could walk to the edge of the world and turn and walk back.

They bathed in the cool river as the light failed, and made their beds on the clean sand of the bank, under the open sky. And here is a thing worth noticing, small but not trivial. These were princes who had slept every night of their lives on soft beds in guarded rooms. That night they lay down on sand, with the river talking beside them and the enormous star-crowded dark overhead, and they were not miserable. They were happy. There is a freedom in the simple life that the palace, for all its comforts, cannot give, and the boys tasted it that first night and never entirely forgot the taste. The forest, which their father had feared for them as a place of only danger, was also this: clean water, open sky, the good tiredness of an honest day, the nearness of a wise man who asked nothing of them but that they grow.

For grow they did, and quickly, and it was the bond between the three of them that grew fastest. On the road there is no rank the way there is in a court. A prince and a sage walking the same dusty miles, eating the same plain food, sleeping under the same trees, come to know one another in a way that palace ceremony never allows. Vishvāmitra, who had come to Ayodhyā as a figure of terror before whom a king had trembled, became to the boys something else on that road: a teacher, yes, and a stern one, but also a companion, a keeper of stories, an old man who noticed when they were footsore and shortened the march without seeming to. And the boys became to him something he had perhaps not expected to feel again after his long solitary austerities: sons of a kind, young lives to pour his knowledge into, a reason to be gentle.

We should let ourselves feel the sweetness of these days, because there will not be many like them. Much of what is coming in this story is hard. There is exile ahead, and abduction, and war, and grief piled on grief. But right here, on the road south, before any of that has begun, there is only a bright morning and three travellers and the whole adventure still ahead of them and none of its cost yet paid. Rāma is not yet the sorrowing exile, not yet the grieving husband, not yet the lonely king. He is a boy on a journey with his brother and his teacher, strong and glad, walking toward the first test of his life with a light step and an easy heart. Let the picture stand a moment before the road carries them on.

Vishvāmitra watched the two of them go ahead of him one morning, laughing at some private joke between brothers, their new mantras making their steps light, and he thought, as old men think watching the young, of all that lay in wait for them down the road, and he did not tell them, because it was not yet time, and because there is a mercy in not knowing. He only followed after, and let them laugh, and kept his knowledge to himself.

The land ahead grew harsher. The green forest gave way to a stretch of dead and blasted country, where nothing grew and the very birds fell silent, and the boys’ laughter died on their lips as they felt the change come over the land. Vishvāmitra’s face grew grave. They had reached the borders of a cursed place, and the first of Rāma’s labours was waiting in it.

Rāma Slays the Monsters

The dead land had a name and a mistress. It was the forest of Tāṭakā, and once, Vishvāmitra told them, it had been as green and living as any country in the world. Now nothing grew there. The trees stood black and leafless, the ground was cracked and grey, and a silence lay over it that was worse than any noise, the silence of a place where living things have learned not to be. The boys felt the wrongness of it in their skin.

“A demoness holds this land,” the sage said. “Tāṭakā. She was not always a monster; she was born beautiful, and had the strength of a thousand elephants given to her as a gift. But strength without goodness is a curse to its owner and everyone near it, and hers turned to cruelty. She and her son have made this whole region a wasteland. They kill travellers, they wreck the hermitages of the sages, they have driven out or devoured every peaceful creature for miles. Rāma, this is your first task. You must kill her.”

Rāma had listened readily to everything the sage had asked of him until now. But at this he hesitated, and the hesitation did him honour. “Kill her, Gurudeva?” he said. “She is a woman. I was taught that a warrior does not raise his hand against a woman, that to do so is among the lowest things a man can do. My whole training rebels against it. How can I do this and remain the man my teachers made me?”

It was not cowardice; nothing in Rāma was ever cowardice. It was the opposite: a young man’s clean instinct for the rule he had been given, a reluctance to become, even for a moment, the kind of man who strikes the weaker. And Vishvāmitra did not scold him for it. A lesser teacher would have snapped at the delay. Vishvāmitra saw that the boy’s hesitation came from the right place, and that the right answer was not to override his conscience but to educate it.

“I honour the instinct that makes you pause,” the sage said. “Never lose it. A man who strikes women easily is a beast. But listen closely, for here is a distinction you must carry all your life. The rule you were taught protects the innocent and the helpless. It exists to shield those who cannot shield themselves. Tāṭakā is neither innocent nor helpless. She has the strength of a thousand elephants and the malice of the pit. She has murdered more travellers than you have years. To stand aside from her because she wears a woman’s shape is not mercy; it is a betrayal of everyone she will kill tomorrow if you spare her today. The question is not whether the creature before you is a man or a woman. The question is whether it is a protector or a predator. A being who has thrown away all righteousness, who lives by preying on the innocent, has stepped outside the protection that righteousness gives, and must be met as what it has made itself. Your duty is not to a rule of combat. Your duty is to the helpless. Do not let a shallow reading of one law make you break the deeper law beneath it.”

Rāma heard this, and understood it, and the understanding settled the matter in him. This is worth marking, because it is the pattern of his whole life. Rāma was never a man who acted without thought and reasoned afterward. When he was troubled by a thing, he needed to see clearly why it was right before he could do it wholly; and once he saw, he acted without a backward glance. His strength was never separate from his understanding. That is what made him more than a warrior.

Tāṭakā came. She had felt the intrusion into her land, and she came roaring out of the dead trees in a fury, a monstrous shape, huge and hideous, hurling boulders and raising storms of dust, her voice alone enough to freeze the blood. She was terrible to behold, and the boys, for all their new mantras and their royal training, were looking at the first real monster of their lives.

But Rāma did not falter now. The time for hesitation was past; he had reasoned his way through it and left it behind. He raised his bow, and where a moment before there had been a troubled boy there was now something else, something that would make demons across the whole southern world learn to fear a single name. He met her charge. The battle was short and furious. She was strong, immensely strong, but strength was not enough against a clear eye and a righteous arm, and Rāma’s arrow found her, and the demoness who had made a wasteland of a living country fell, and was still.

And the moment she died, the land felt it. The wrongness that had hung over the place lifted like a weight taken off the chest. The killing of Tāṭakā was not a cruelty; it was a healing. In time, the tellers say, the blasted forest would grow green again, the birds would come back, travellers would walk the road unafraid. One life, rightly ended, gave life back to a whole country. This is the hard arithmetic of the protector, and Rāma had learned to do the sum.

Vishvāmitra was pleased, and he showed his pleasure in the way a great teacher does: by giving the pupil more. He bestowed on Rāma a whole armoury of celestial weapons, the divine astras, missiles of fire and wind and light that answered to sacred words, weapons the gods themselves had wielded. Rāma received them gravely, and Vishvāmitra watched him receive them and was satisfied that they had come into safe hands, for the boy showed no greed for them, no eagerness to use them, only a sober sense of what such power meant.

Then they went on, to the true purpose of the journey: the sacrifice. They came to Vishvāmitra’s hermitage, the Siddhāshrama, and the sage made his preparations, and told the boys their task. “For six days and nights I will be bound by the rite, unable to lift a hand. On the last day the demons will come, Mārīcha and Subāhu, to defile the fire with blood and flesh at the very moment of its completion. That is when you must guard me. Watch the sky. Let nothing reach the altar.”

They watched. For six days the sacrifice rose toward its completion, the chanting unbroken, the fire fed, the sage lost in his devotions. And on the last day, as Vishvāmitra had foretold, the sky darkened, and the demons came, screaming down out of the clouds with a rain of filth to ruin the holy work at its final hour.

But the boys were ready. Rāma loosed a weapon at Mārīcha, not the killing shaft, for something stayed his hand toward that one, but a weapon that struck the demon like a mountain and flung him far out across the miles, hurling him bodily into the distant sea, stunned but living. Mārīcha would remember that blow. It would matter later, in a way none of them could yet see. And upon Subāhu, Rāma loosed the weapon of fire, and Subāhu was consumed and fell to ash, and the lesser demons that came behind them were scattered like leaves before a gale. The altar was untouched. The sacrifice reached its completion clean and whole, and the fire rose up pure at the end, and the sages of the hermitage lifted their voices in a joy they had not felt in years, for their fire was safe at last and the long torment of their rite was ended.

Vishvāmitra came out of his devotions to find his sacrifice complete and his young guardians standing watch over an unspoiled altar, and he blessed them both. The first labour was done, and done well, and the boy who had hesitated to raise his hand against a woman had learned the hardest lesson a protector learns: that mercy misplaced is only cruelty postponed, and that the truest kindness is sometimes the firm and terrible hand that ends an evil before it can feed again.

Sītā

With the sacrifice safely completed, Vishvāmitra’s purpose in bringing the princes was fulfilled. But he did not send them home. There was another thing he meant them to see, though he did not tell them so directly, for the best teachers arrange the lesson and let the pupil walk into it. He turned their steps not north toward Ayodhyā but further on, toward the kingdom of the north, toward Mithilā, where a king named Janaka ruled and a great event was about to take place.

As they travelled, the sage spoke of Janaka, and it is worth our while to listen, for Janaka was no ordinary monarch. He was a philosopher-king, one of those rare men who wear a crown and yet are not owned by it. He ruled his kingdom well, with justice and with care, and at the same time he had gone as deep into the questions of the spirit as any forest hermit. The sages honoured him not as a patron but as a peer. It was said that Janaka had reached a state where he could hold the whole business of kingship, its wealth and its wars and its ceremonies, in an open hand, neither grasping it nor throwing it away, present to all of it and attached to none. He was in the world and not of it, and this is one of the hardest things a human being can be, harder by far in a palace than in a cave, and Janaka managed it in a palace.

And it was to this king, years before, that a strange and beautiful gift had come.

Janaka had been performing a sacrifice, and part of the rite required him to plough a strip of sacred ground with his own royal hands, for even a king, in the presence of the holy, takes up the labourer’s work. As he drove the plough down the consecrated furrow, the blade struck something in the earth, and he stopped, and looked, and found in the opened ground a child. A baby girl, lying in the furrow as though the earth itself had lifted her up and offered her to him, perfect and unharmed and gazing up at the astonished king.

She had no mother that any man knew, no father, no lineage that could be traced. She had come from the earth, from the furrow, from the ploughed line itself, and so Janaka named her Sītā, which is the word for that very furrow. She was, the tellers say and the faithful believe, no ordinary foundling but a descent, as Rāma was a descent, the Goddess herself taking human form and human infancy, come into the world by the strangest and gentlest of doors to meet the one who had come to meet her. But Janaka did not know this, or did not need to. He knew only that the earth had given him a daughter, and he took her up out of the furrow and into his heart, and he loved her from that first moment as no natural father ever loved a natural child.

And she grew, in the palace at Mithilā, into a girl of such grace and such quiet strength that those around her felt it without being able to name it. There was in her, from her earliest years, a self-possession that did not come from her upbringing, for it was there before her upbringing could have put it there. She was gentle, and she was immovable, and the two lived together in her without contradiction, the way they lived in Rāma. Perhaps that is why the story was always going to bring them together. Some meetings are prepared long before they happen.

There is a tale of her childhood that Janaka loved to tell, and it foreshadows everything. In the treasury of Mithilā there was kept a great bow, the bow of Shiva himself, an object of immense sacred power and enormous weight, so heavy that it took hundreds of men to move the cart it rested on. It was not a thing anyone touched. It sat in its place, honoured and untouchable, the most fearsome relic in the kingdom.

One day, when Sītā was still a small child, a ball she was playing with rolled beneath the great bow’s pedestal. And Sītā, thinking nothing of it, being a child who wanted her ball, walked over, took hold of the pedestal that grown men could not shift, lifted it aside as easily as if it were a stool, retrieved her ball, and went back to her game.

The court that witnessed it went silent with awe. Janaka understood, in that moment, that his daughter was not what she appeared to be, that the earth had given him something more than a child. And he made a vow, there and then, about her marriage. He would not give her to any man merely for his rank or his riches or the alliance he offered. The girl who had lifted Shiva’s bow with one small hand would be given only to a man who could match that strength, a man worthy of her origin and her nature. Let the bow be the test, he declared. Whoever among all the kings and princes of the earth could lift that mighty bow and string it would win the hand of Sītā. And until such a man came, she would not be given at all.

Years passed, and no such man came. Kings tried and failed. Great warriors, proud of their strength, came to Mithilā to attempt the bow and went away humbled, unable even to stir it in its rest. The vow began to look less like a wise condition and more like a wall, and Janaka, who loved his daughter and wished to see her happily settled, began quietly to wonder whether he had asked for a thing the world could not supply.

And now, as our story returns to the road, Janaka had proclaimed a great assembly, a gathering of kings, one more contest of the bow. From every quarter the mighty were coming to Mithilā to try their strength, and the whole kingdom was astir with it. This was the event toward which Vishvāmitra was quietly steering two boys from Ayodhyā, one of whom was strong beyond the reckoning of any king on earth, and neither of whom yet knew that a girl born from a furrow was waiting at the end of the road.

The sage said nothing of any of this. He only led them north, and told them stories, and let the road carry them toward the meeting that the earth and the fire had been preparing since before either child was born. But before Mithilā there was one more hermitage to pass, one more soul waiting by the way, and her story is among the tenderest in the whole telling, and it deserves a chapter of its own.

Bhagīratha and the Story of Gangā

Their road to Mithilā crossed a river, and it was no ordinary river. It was the Gangā herself, the holiest of all waters, and as they waited to cross, Rāma asked the sage how it came to be that a river should be worshipped as a goddess and a mother. Vishvāmitra sat them down on the bank, and told them, and the story he told is one of the great stories, a story of ashes and of patience, of a fault that ran through five generations and the single man who at last made it right.

It began with a king named Sagara, a mighty ruler of Rāma’s own line, the house of Ikshvāku. Sagara had two wives but for long had no children, and after great penances he was granted a strange boon: from one wife, a single son who would carry on the line; from the other, sixty thousand sons. And so it was. Sixty thousand princes were born to Sagara, a host of them, filling his kingdom with their number.

But sixty thousand sons, all born together, all proud, all raised as princes, are a difficult blessing. They grew up strong and brave, but they grew up arrogant, too many to be corrected, too sure of their own might. And here is the first thread of the lesson: a gift can become a burden if it is not matched by wisdom. Sagara had asked for many sons and received them, and never thought to ask that they be good ones.

Sagara resolved to perform the Ashvamedha, the horse-sacrifice, the grandest of all rites, by which a king declares his sovereignty over the earth. In this rite a consecrated horse is set free to wander where it will for a year, and wherever it goes, that land acknowledges the king’s supremacy, and at the year’s end the horse is brought home and sacrificed. But Indra, king of the gods, for reasons of his own, was unwilling to let the rite succeed, and he stole the horse in secret and hid it away, deep in the netherworld, tethered near the hermitage of a great sage named Kapila, who sat there sunk in a meditation so deep he knew nothing of the world around him.

When the horse went missing, Sagara sent his sixty thousand sons to find it, and they set about the search in exactly the way you would expect of sixty thousand arrogant princes: not with humility, but with force. They tore up the earth. They dug down through the ground itself, ripping open the world in their search, until they came at last to the netherworld and found the horse tethered there, and near it the sage Kapila, sitting silent in his trance. And here they made the error that destroyed them. Seeing the horse beside the sage, they leapt to the easy, insulting conclusion: this hermit is the thief. They did not pause. They did not ask. They rushed upon the meditating sage with shouts and weapons, hurling accusations, ready to seize him as a common horse-thief.

Kapila opened his eyes. That was all. He had not stolen the horse; he had not even known it was there; he had been wronged, insulted, set upon by an arrogant mob who could not be troubled to ask a question before they drew a blade. And the power of a great sage’s gaze, disturbed from deep meditation and meeting such insolence, was a terrible thing. From his eyes there came a heat, and in an instant, all sixty thousand of Sagara’s sons were burned to ash where they stood. A whole host of princes, the pride of a great king, reduced in a heartbeat to grey heaps of ash on the floor of the netherworld.

Let us feel the weight of that, and the justice threaded through the tragedy. The sons were not destroyed for searching, nor for their strength. They were destroyed for their arrogance, for the deadly readiness to accuse and to strike before they understood. Kapila had done no wrong; their own rush to judgment was the fire that consumed them. How much sorrow in this world comes from exactly that fault, the leap to blame, the blow struck before the question is asked. The sixty thousand are a warning written very large.

But the tragedy did not end with their death, for they had died wrongly, unpurified, their rites unperformed, and so their souls could find no rest. They were stranded, neither living nor at peace, held in a grey limbo, and they would remain so until the holy waters of heaven, the Gangā, who then flowed only in the sky, could be brought down to earth and made to flow over their ashes and release them.

And this became the burden of the family, passed down like a debt. Sagara himself could not bring the river down, though he tried. His heir could not, nor could his heir’s son. Generation after generation laboured at the impossible task and failed and died and passed the sorrow to their children, the ashes of the sixty thousand still lying unredeemed, the souls still waiting. It is a hard thing to inherit a debt you did not incur, to be born already owing a labour you did not choose. But so it is, sometimes, in families and in nations both: the faults of one generation become the burden of the next, and someone, at last, must pay what the first fault cost.

The one who paid was Bhagīratha.

He was born, generations later, into that inheritance, and he did not shrug it off. He might have. He might have said, reasonably enough, that the sin was not his, that the arrogant princes had brought their fate on themselves, that a man cannot spend his life redeeming the dead. Instead he looked at the unfinished labour of his whole line and he took it up as his own. He gave his kingdom into the care of his ministers, and he went alone into the mountains, and he began a penance the like of which had rarely been seen.

He stood, the tellers say, on one leg, through summer and winter, through burning sun and freezing wind, surviving on air alone, his whole being bent upon a single prayer: that the Gangā might come down from heaven and free his ancestors at last. Years he stood so. The flesh wasted from his bones and still he stood, unmoving, unwavering, offering the one thing a determined soul can always offer, which is everything it has, held out for as long as it takes.

And such determination, held long enough and purely enough, moves even heaven. Brahmā came to him first, and granted that the Gangā would descend. But there was a difficulty, and it was a grave one. The Gangā’s fall from heaven would be so vast, so violent, so heavy with the weight of the celestial waters, that the earth could not survive the impact. She would smash the world to pieces where she landed. Some power had to receive that fall and break it, and only one being in all the worlds was mighty enough to do so: Lord Shiva himself.

So Bhagīratha, his first prayer answered, began a second, praying now to Shiva to catch the falling river. And Shiva, moved by the same unshakable devotion, consented. He took his stand upon the earth and let the Gangā fall upon his head, and she came down in her full heavenly fury, meaning perhaps to sweep even the great god away with her, and she vanished into the vast matted locks of his hair and was lost there, wandering in that endless labyrinth, her pride and her violence swallowed and gentled. Only when Bhagīratha prayed once more did Shiva release her, and now she came forth not as a catastrophe but as a river, divided into gentle streams, tamed, blessed, fit to flow upon the earth without destroying it.

And Bhagīratha went before her. On his chariot he led the way, and the Gangā followed him, faithfully, wherever he went, down from the mountains and across the plains, all the long way to the sea and then down into the netherworld itself, to the place where the grey ashes of the sixty thousand still waited. And her holy waters flowed over them at last, and the long-stranded souls were purified and released, and rose, freed, after all those generations, into peace.

“That is why she is called Bhagirathi as well as Gangā,” Vishvāmitra finished, “after the man whose patience brought her down. And that is why, when you cross her waters, you cross something more than a river. You cross a redemption that took five generations and one man’s whole life to accomplish.”

The boys were quiet, looking at the moving water with new eyes. Rāma, who was of the same line as Sagara and Bhagīratha, looked longest. There was a lesson in it shaped exactly for him, though neither he nor the sage said so aloud: that the highest work is often the redeeming of an inherited sorrow, that duty is sometimes a debt we did not run up but must pay all the same, and that patience, mere patience, held past all reason and all comfort, is among the mightiest forces in the world. He would need every part of that lesson. But not yet. For now there was only the holy river, and the road beyond it, and Mithilā waiting with its bow and its furrow-born daughter, one long day’s journey to the north.

Ahalyā

Before Mithilā there was one more hermitage on their road, and Rāma felt its strangeness before he understood it. They came upon a grove of grey and silent trees, an ashram that had plainly once been tended and was now abandoned, the ground still bearing the faint shape of paths no feet had walked in years. Nothing lived there. No birds sang in the grey branches. There was a stillness over the place that was not peace but something closer to holding of breath, as though the grove itself were waiting for something.

“Why does this ashram stand empty and neglected, Gurudeva?” Rāma asked. “It was clearly the home of a holy man once. What drove the life out of it?”

Vishvāmitra stopped, and looked at the silent trees, and his voice when he answered was gentler than usual. “This was the hermitage of the sage Gautama,” he said, “and of his wife, Ahalyā. And there is a sorrow here, a very old one, and it is nearly ended, though the ending waits on you. Listen, and do not judge too quickly, for the story asks more of our compassion than of our condemnation.”

Ahalyā, he told them, had been a woman of extraordinary beauty and, more than that, of real virtue, the devoted wife of a great and austere sage. And Indra, the king of the gods, conceived a desire for her, a desire he had no right to and should have mastered and did not. This is a thing worth pausing on before we go further: that even among the gods, desire ungoverned is the root of ruin, and that high place and great power are no protection against the oldest of failings. Indra had heaven itself, and it was not enough, because a heart that will not discipline its wanting is never given enough.

Indra came to the hermitage by a deceit. Knowing the hour when Gautama would be away at his morning devotions by the river, he took upon himself the very form of the sage, Gautama’s face, Gautama’s voice, Gautama’s manner, and in that borrowed shape he came to Ahalyā.

Here the tellers of the story differ, and it is honest to say so. Some hold that Ahalyā was wholly deceived, that she believed she received her own husband and bore no guilt at all. Others hold that in some part of her she sensed the deceit and faltered for a moment, dazzled that the king of the gods should desire her so. The story does not fully resolve it, and perhaps it is not meant to, for the truth of the human heart in such a moment is rarely clean, and a tale that pretended otherwise would be a lesser and a falser tale. What is certain is this: that a wrong was done, and that whatever Ahalyā’s share in it, the deceit was Indra’s and the greater fault was his.

Gautama returned. And a sage of his power was not to be fooled; he saw at once what had happened, and the sight broke something in him. His wrath was terrible, and it fell in two directions. Upon Indra he laid a curse that humbled the king of the gods before all the worlds. And upon Ahalyā, his own wife, he laid a curse that has troubled the conscience of everyone who has ever heard this story, and is meant to.

She would remain in this grove, he decreed, invisible to all eyes, formless, lying in the dust and the ash, taking neither food nor water but only the air, alone in the emptiness, for uncounted thousands of years. She would neither die nor truly live. She would simply endure, unseen, unremembered, wearing away the debt in silence and in dust. And there was only one term set to it, one distant mercy folded into the harshness: the penance would end, and her form return, on the day that Rāma, the prince of Ayodhyā, should set his foot in the grove.

“And so,” Vishvāmitra said quietly, “she has waited. Longer than kingdoms last. Longer than the memory of men. She has lain here in the dust of this grove through the fall of ages, formless and alone, holding to the one promise that someday a certain foot would cross this ground. That is why the trees are grey and the birds are silent. They are keeping watch with her. And Rāma, the foot she has waited for is yours. Step forward.”

We should let ourselves feel the enormity of that waiting before Rāma takes the step. Think of what it is to endure, alone and unseen, not for a year or a lifetime but for ages, sustained by nothing but a promise so distant it must have seemed less a hope than a legend. If there was fault in Ahalyā, it was a fault of a single hour; the penance was the length of the world. And she did not break. She did not curse her husband, or rail against heaven, or let bitterness eat the last of her. She waited, and kept faith, and wore the wrong away with the sheer patient endurance of a soul that would not give up its hope. There is a kind of strength in that which the strength of warriors never touches.

Rāma stepped forward into the courtyard of the grove.

And where his foot came down, the long penance ended. The dust stirred. The grey air trembled. And slowly, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud, a form gathered itself out of the emptiness, faint at first and then clearer, until Ahalyā stood before them, restored, radiant, her long ordeal fallen away from her like a shed garment. She was as she had been, and more, for the ages of patient suffering had burned something clean in her, and there was a light in her that had not been there before the sorrow.

She looked upon Rāma, and she understood who he was, for the one whose foot could end her curse could be no ordinary prince. And Rāma looked upon her, not with judgment, not with the least shadow of the condemnation that a smaller soul might have carried, but with pure and simple compassion, honouring her, offering her the reverence due to one who had suffered so long and so faithfully. He did not come to her as a judge weighing an old sin. He came as the one appointed to end her sorrow, and he ended it, and asked nothing.

And here is the heart of it, the thing this beautiful and difficult episode exists to teach. The divine does not come into the world to catch us in our worst hour and hold it against us forever. It comes to redeem, to restore, to lift the fallen back to their feet and give them their true form again. Ahalyā’s story is not finally a story about a sin. It is a story about grace, about the mercy that meets long suffering not with a fresh accusation but with a hand extended, about the truth that no one is beyond the reach of redemption if only they will endure and keep faith. The dust does not have the last word. The compassion that comes at the end of the long waiting has the last word.

Gautama himself returned then, his long anger at last spent, the term of the curse fulfilled, and husband and wife were reunited in the grove, restored to one another after the ages of separation. And the grey trees, the tellers say, put out their first green in uncounted years, and somewhere in the branches a single bird tried its voice again, tentatively, as though remembering how. The grove that had held its breath so long could breathe once more.

The travellers left them there together, in their renewed and quiet peace, and went on toward Mithilā. And Rāma carried the picture of it with him: the form gathering out of the dust, the light of one who had suffered and kept faith, the whole grief of ages ended by the crossing of a threshold. He did not know yet how much he too would one day have to endure, or how heavily the questions raised in that grove, of a wife’s honour, of public judgment, of the terrible cost of another’s suspicion, would one day fall upon his own house. The story was showing him something, early and gently, that it would ask him to live through, hard and to the bone, before the end.

Rāma Wins Sītā’s Hand

They came at last to Mithilā, and the city was full. From every kingdom of the earth the mighty had gathered, kings and princes and famous warriors, drawn by Janaka’s proclamation and the prize it offered. The streets thronged with retinues and banners; the inns overflowed; the whole capital hummed with the particular excitement of a great contest whose outcome no one could foresee. And at the centre of it all, in the courtyard of the palace, waited the bow.

It rested on an eight-wheeled iron cart, and the cart alone was a thing to marvel at, for it took five hundred strong men to drag it into place. The bow itself lay upon it like a sleeping thing, immense, ancient, radiating a sacred weight that made men lower their voices near it. This was Shiva’s bow, and every king in that courtyard knew its history and knew the vow attached to it: lift it, string it, and win the hand of the princess Sītā; fail, and go home shamed before the assembled world.

When Vishvāmitra came into the court leading two young men in the simple garments of forest travellers, no one paid them much attention. The great ones were there, the celebrated strong men, the kings whose names were sung. Who were these two boys walking behind an old sage? Janaka received Vishvāmitra with deep respect, as was due to so great a rishi, and the sage asked, almost mildly, whether the young prince with him might be permitted to look upon the famous bow. Janaka, courteous and a little sorrowful, agreed, though one imagines he expected nothing. He had watched so many strong men fail. He had begun, we know, to fear that his vow had shut his daughter away from any possible husband.

For the contest had already been going badly, and for a long time. One after another the mighty had come forward to try the bow, and one after another they had been humbled. Great kings, proud of a lifetime’s strength, had set their hands to it and strained until the veins stood out on their necks and could not stir it in its rest. Whole teams of warriors had heaved at it together and failed to lift it a finger’s breadth. The thing simply would not be moved by ordinary might, however great. And with each failure a kind of gloom had settled deeper over the court, and over Janaka most of all, for every failure seemed to seal his daughter’s solitude more firmly.

Let us understand what made this moment so heavy, for it was not only about strength. Janaka had made a vow, and a king’s vow cannot be unmade, and he had begun to see that his vow, made in love and in awe of his daughter’s nature, might have become a wall around her that no one on earth could pass. This is a thing that happens to good intentions: they harden into conditions, and the conditions outlast the love that made them, and we find ourselves imprisoned by our own high standards. Janaka loved Sītā and wanted her happy, and he had bound her happiness to a feat that seemed beyond the reach of the whole world. He watched the young forest prince walk toward the bow with, one supposes, more courtesy than hope.

Rāma came before the great bow and bowed to it, for it was a sacred thing and he honoured sacred things. Then, with no display, no visible summoning of effort, no straining, he set his hand to it.

The court had grown silent. Every eye was on the slight young figure and the enormous weapon.

Rāma lifted the bow.

He lifted it as easily as a man lifts a walking-staff, raised that immensity that five hundred men had labored to drag, raised it smoothly into the air, and the silence in the court became the silence of held breath. And then, to string it, he bent it, drew the great arc of it toward himself to fasten the cord.

And the bow broke.

It could not bear the strength that bent it. With a sound like a thunderclap directly overhead, a sound that split the air and rolled out across the whole city and shook the ground, the ancient bow of Shiva snapped in two in Rāma’s hands. Men cried out and clapped their hands to their ears. Birds burst up from every roof in Mithilā. And in the ringing silence that followed the enormous crack, the whole assembly understood at once that they had witnessed something they would tell their grandchildren, that the impossible condition had been met, and met not with grunting effort but with an ease that was somehow more astonishing than any struggle could have been.

Janaka rose from his seat with his face transformed. The gloom of the long failed contest fell from him in an instant. His daughter’s long solitude was over; and better than that, far better, she was won not by some brute of mere muscle but by this, this young prince of grace and gentleness and quiet overwhelming strength, exactly the union of power and goodness that Janaka in his deepest hope had wanted for her and had almost stopped believing existed. He came down to Rāma with tears in his eyes.

And Sītā. The tellers say she had watched from among the women of the court, and that when the bow broke and she understood who had broken it, something in her that had been waiting as long as Rāma’s own destiny had waited quietly came home. She had lifted that bow’s pedestal herself, as a child, with one hand; she of all people knew what strength lay sleeping in it; and here was the one being on earth whose strength answered hers. When she came forward, at the proper time, to place the garland of victory around the neck of the man who had won her, it was not the shy submission of a girl handed to a stranger. It was a meeting. Two who had come into the world from strange doors, the furrow and the fire, the earth and the flame, recognizing one another at last. The garland settled on Rāma’s shoulders, and a thing that had been prepared since before either of them was born was accomplished.

Messengers rode north at once to Ayodhyā, and Dasharatha came, overjoyed, with his whole court and his other three sons, to celebrate his eldest boy’s marriage. And Janaka, whose generosity now overflowed as his sorrow had once weighed him down, offered not one union but four. For he had a second daughter, Ūrmilā, and his brother had two daughters besides, Māṇḍavī and Shrutakīrti, and it was arranged, in the joy of that great meeting of families, that all four princes of Ayodhyā should be wed to the four princesses of Mithilā together. Ūrmilā to Lakshmaṇa, Māṇḍavī to Bharata, Shrutakīrti to Shatrughna, and Sītā to Rāma.

And so there was a wedding such as the world had rarely seen. For days Mithilā was a single festival, the sacred fires kindled, the mantras chanted, the four young couples circling the flame that makes a marriage, the streets running with music and light and the scattering of flowers. Two royal houses were joined; four brothers who were one soul in four bodies were wedded on the same day; and the whole of it was crowned by the union at its centre, Rāma and Sītā, the descent of Nārāyaṇa and the descent of the Goddess, come together in human form to walk a human road that neither of them yet knew would run through such long darkness before it came home to the light.

But on that day there was no darkness, only the fire and the flowers and the joined hands and the enormous gladness of two families and two kingdoms. Dasharatha wept for happiness. Janaka, who had feared his daughter would never be given, gave her with a full heart. And the four couples turned about the sacred flame while the city sang. It was, all agreed, the most auspicious of beginnings.

The road home to Ayodhyā still held one more trial, one last shadow to cross before they reached the city. But the wedding itself was pure joy, unshadowed, complete, and it is right to let it stand so, bright and whole, before the story asks its people to begin paying the long price of their greatness. · · ·

Parashurāma’s Discomfiture

The wedding done, the great company set out north for Ayodhyā, a long joyful procession of two royal houses newly joined, the four young couples at its heart, Dasharatha’s cup of happiness filled to the brim. He had come to Mithilā fearing for the son Vishvāmitra had taken from him, and he was returning with that son grown into a hero, married to a bride from heaven, the future of his line secured in a single stroke. The old king rode home the happiest man in the world.

But the earth was not done testing them, and the last test of the Bāla Kāṇḍa came without warning.

The sky darkened. A wind rose that was not a natural wind, and the ground began to tremble, and the horses screamed and shied, and a terror fell over the whole procession as some vast and furious presence approached. And then he was there, blocking the road: a figure out of an older and harder age, matted-haired, blazing-eyed, an axe upon his shoulder and a great bow in his hand, and the very air around him seemed to burn. It was Parashurāma.

Now Parashurāma was a name to freeze the blood of any warrior, and every man in that procession knew it. He was of an earlier turning of the age, a brahmin by birth who had taken up the weapons of a warrior for a terrible purpose. The warrior-caste of that age had grown arrogant and cruel, oppressing the earth, and Parashurāma had made a vow to humble them, and he had kept it with a fury that had become legend. Twenty-one times, the tellers say, he had cleared the earth of the proud warrior-kings, axe in hand, an exterminating wrath that had washed the world in blood. And here he stood, this ancient and merciless force, planted in the road before the wedding party, and the joy of the procession curdled into dread.

He had heard, it seemed, of the breaking of Shiva’s bow, and it had brought him. He came straight toward Rāma, and his voice was like the grinding of mountains. So, he said in effect, a boy has broken the bow of Shiva and thinks himself a hero. Here is another bow, the bow of Vishṇu, greater still, the companion of that other. Let the boy string this one, if he can, and we shall see what he is truly made of; and let him understand that this is no wedding game but a reckoning.

Dasharatha’s new-won happiness shattered in an instant. The old king flung himself forward, pleading, offering himself, offering anything, begging this terror out of the deep past to spare his son. He had feared to lose Rāma to Vishvāmitra’s demons and had gotten him back; he had feared and hoped through the whole contest of the bow; and now, on the very road home, with all his happiness gathered around him, here was death itself standing in the path reaching for his boy. The father in him could not bear it, and he wept and pleaded in the road, a king unkinged by fear for his child.

But Rāma was not afraid.

This is the thing to hold onto in the scene, the contrast at its heart: all around him grown men trembled and his own royal father wept in the dust, and Rāma stood calm. He did not answer the ancient warrior’s fury with fury of his own. He was courteous, even gentle, and utterly unshaken. He heard Parashurāma out, and then he simply reached and took the great bow of Vishṇu from the raging sage’s hand, took it as easily as he had taken up Shiva’s bow in Mithilā, and strung it, and drew it, all without effort, all without heat, while the fearsome figure who had cleared the earth of kings watched his weapon pass into the young man’s hands and be mastered.

And as Rāma strung the bow of Vishṇu, something happened in Parashurāma. The fury went out of him. For this was the thing he had not understood, the thing the whole encounter existed to reveal: that the age of his wrath was ending, and a new age was beginning, and that the very power he had carried, the cosmic force of righteous destruction, was now passing out of his hands and into the hands of the one who stood before him. Parashurāma had been an instrument, mighty and terrible, of the divine will in his turning of the age; and now the divine had come into the world itself, in this calm young prince, and the instrument’s work was done. He felt his own long violence recognize its successor and its master. The blazing eyes dimmed. The proud shoulders bowed.

For the arrow was already fitted to the drawn bow of Vishṇu, and such a shaft, once fitted and drawn, could not simply be set aside; it had to be loosed somewhere, spent upon some target. And Rāma, with the great weapon bent and ready in his hands and the humbled sage before him, did not turn it upon Parashurāma. He asked, courteously, where he should send it, since it could not be withheld. And Parashurāma, wholly quieted now, yielded up to the arrow the accumulated merit of his own penances, or by other tellings the power of his further movement through the worlds, so that the shaft was spent upon that and not upon his life. His age was over. He gave what he had to give to the one who had superseded him, and withdrew from the world of action into the long quiet of penance, and troubled the earth no more. The terror passed. The sky cleared. The wind fell, and the horses grew calm, and the ground was steady underfoot again, and the procession stood blinking in the returned daylight, hardly able to believe that the ancient death which had blocked their road had been faced down and dissolved by a young man who never once raised his voice.

Dasharatha gathered his son to him, weak with relief, and the tellers say he understood in that moment, more than he had understood even at the breaking of Shiva’s bow, that the child he had feared for was beyond his power to protect, because the child had never needed his protection; that something had come into his house that was larger than his house, larger than his kingdom, larger than his understanding. He had wanted a son to carry on his line. He had been given the Lord of the worlds to call his own. It was joy and it was awe and it was, though he could not have named it then, the beginning of a letting-go that would break his heart before it was done.

But that was still to come. For now the last shadow of the Bāla Kāṇḍa had lifted, and the road ran clear and bright before them all the way home. They came to Ayodhyā in triumph and in gladness, the city poured out to meet them, and the four young couples came home to a capital wild with joy. Rāma and Sītā came into the palace that had waited so long first for Rāma’s birth and now for his bride, and the whole of Ayodhyā settled into what everyone believed would be a long, golden, unshadowed happiness.

And for twelve years, it was.

ta.title: பாலகாண்டம்: தெய்வீக தொடக்கங்கள்
ta.body:
கருவுறுதல்

எல்லாம் நிறைந்திருப்பவர்களை மட்டுமே தேடிவரும் ஒரு துயரம் உண்டு. அயோத்தியின் அரசன் தசரதன் அந்தத் துயரத்தை நன்கு அறிந்திருந்தான்.

அக்காலத்தில் அயோத்தி உலகின் மிகச் செழிப்பான நகரங்களில் ஒன்றாக விளங்கியது. அதன் தெருக்கள் அகன்று தூய்மையாக இருந்தன, தானியக் களஞ்சியங்கள் பொன்னிற தானியங்களால் நிறைந்திருந்தன, மக்கள் அமைதியிலும் பரஸ்பர மரியாதையிலும் வாழ்ந்தனர். சரயூ நதி அதன் மதில்களைத் தழுவிச் சென்று, கோயில் கொடிகளின் பிரதிபலிப்பையும் ஆயிரம் மாலை விளக்குகளின் புகையையும் தன் மேற்பரப்பில் சுமந்து சென்றது. பழம்பெரும் இக்ஷ்வாகு வம்சத்தைச் சேர்ந்த தசரத மன்னன், தன் அமைச்சர்களின் வழிகாட்டுதலோடும், தன் குலகுருவான மகரிஷி வசிஷ்டரின் அருளோடும் இச்செழிப்பான அரசை ஆண்டு வந்தான். ஒரு காலத்தில் தேவர்களுடன் சேர்ந்து அசுரர்களை எதிர்த்துப் போரிட்டிருந்த அவனுக்குச் செல்வமும் புகழும் வெற்றிகளும் இருந்தன. அவனுக்கு எதுவும் குறையவில்லை.
